```{r}
#| label: footer-options

options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
```

Here we present all available options for the priors and Monte Carlo proposals in housepi.

# Continuous priors

To perform the sampling we consider the "test" model (i.e. a dummy template with no transmission model, see `?template_test`).
The continuous distributions in housepi are:
```{r}
#| label: continuous-priors-density
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Density plots for prior distributions available in housepi for Bayesian inference: uniform, normal, lognormal, gamma, Weibull, Rayleigh, beta, exponential and loguniform.
#|  Each panel displays the estimated probability density function in blue obtained from MCMC sampling.
library(housepi)
set_housepi_theme(colour_strips = TRUE)
set.seed(42)

# create an instance of the model 'test'
new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  # continuous distributions in housepi
  add_parameter(uniform = list(prior = "uniform", min = 0, max = 1),
                normal = list(prior = "normal", mean = 0, sd = 1),
                lognormal = list(prior = "lognormal", meanlog = 0, sdlog = 1),
                gamma = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1),
                weibull = list(prior = "weibull", shape = 2, scale = 1),
                rayleigh = list(prior = "rayleigh", scale = 1),
                beta = list(prior = "beta", shape1 = 2, shape2 = 1),
                exponential = list(prior = "exponential", rate = 1),
                loguniform = list(prior = "loguniform", min = 0.01, max = 1)) |>
  # perform the sampling with the inference command
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens()
```
Here we associated definitions of parameters with default proposals and custom arguments.
Argument defaults match the base R sampling functions (e.g. `normal` starts from `mean = 0` and `sd = 1` as in `rnorm()`).
Arguments carrying no default in base R stay required in housepi too.

# Provide a custom domain

The arguments `min` (minimum) and `max` (maximum) set a custom support for a variable, truncating its distribution.
```{r}
#| label: truncation-demo
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Four density plots demonstrating truncation options for normal distribution.
#|  Orange dashed lines indicate truncation boundaries applied to distributions.
library(ggplot2)

new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(default = list(prior = "normal"),
                below = list(prior = "normal", min = -1),
                above = list(prior = "normal", max = 1),
                both = list(prior = "normal", min = -1, max = 1)) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-3, 3), ylim = c(0, 0.65)) +
  geom_vline(data = data.frame(Parameter = c("below", "above", "both", "both"),
                               xintercept = c(-1, 1, -1, 1)),
             aes(xintercept = xintercept),
             linetype = 2)
```

# Provide a location parameter

All functions and distributions in housepi allow for a location parameter `loc` to translate the support of the distribution:
```{r}
#| label: location-parameter-demo
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Density plots showing gamma distributions with different location parameters.
#|  Four panels display gamma distributions with location parameters set to 0, 1, 2, and 3 respectively.
#|  Vertical dashed lines indicate the minimum of each shifted support.
new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(g0 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2),
                g1 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, loc = 1),
                g2 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, loc = 2),
                g3 = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, loc = 3)) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_dens() +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10)) +
  geom_vline(data = data.frame(Parameter = c("g0", "g1", "g2", "g3"),
                               xintercept = c(0, 1, 2, 3)),
             aes(xintercept = xintercept),
             linetype = 2)
```

# Discrete priors

```{r}
#| label: color-scheme-discrete
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "orange")
```

The discrete distributions in housepi are:
```{r}
#| label: discrete-priors-hist
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Five histograms displaying discrete prior distributions available in housepi: poisson, binomial, negative binomial, geometric, and categorical.
#|  Orange bars represent probability mass functions for integer-valued outcomes obtained from MCMC sampling.

# discrete distributions in housepi
new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(
    poisson = list(prior = "poisson", lambda = 2),
    binomial = list(prior = "binomial", size = 4, prob = 0.5),
    negative_binomial = list(prior = "negative_binomial", size = 4, prob = 0.5),
    geometric = list(prior = "geometric", prob = 0.5),
    categorical = list(prior = "categorical", low = 0.3, mid = 0.1, high = 0.6)
  ) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_hist(binwidth = 1)
```

# Discretize continuous priors

Any continuous prior can be discretized with the argument `discr`.
A discretized distribution gives each integer `k` the probability between `k` and `k + 1`.
```{r}
#| label: discretized-priors-hist
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Seven histograms showing discretized versions of continuous prior distributions: uniform, normal, lognormal, gamma, Weibull, Rayleigh, and exponential.

new_housepi_model(model = "test") |>
  add_parameter(uniform = list(prior = "uniform", discr = TRUE),
                normal = list(prior = "normal", discr = TRUE),
                lognormal = list(prior = "lognormal", discr = TRUE),
                gamma = list(prior = "gamma", shape = 2, discr = TRUE),
                weibull = list(prior = "weibull", shape = 2, discr = TRUE),
                rayleigh = list(prior = "rayleigh", discr = TRUE),
                exponential = list(prior = "exponential", discr = TRUE)) |>
  run_inference() |>
  get_parameter_draws() |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_hist(binwidth = 1)
```
Here we dropped all arguments that have a default value (see above).

## Discretization in practice

We use the function `browse_distributions` to return a distribution object from housepi and explore its methods.
```{r}
#| label: discretization-scheme-plot
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Histogram illustrating the discretization scheme as average probability.
gamma_cont <- browse_distributions("gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1)
gamma_discr <- browse_distributions("gamma", shape = 2, scale = 1, discr = TRUE)

dplyr::tibble(x = seq(0, 9, 1), y = gamma_discr$pdf(x),
              z1 = gamma_cont$cdf(x + 1), z0 = gamma_cont$cdf(x)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin  = x, xmax  = x + 1,
                ymin  = 0, ymax  = z1 - z0, fill  = "average_prob"),
            color = "coral") +
  geom_point(aes(x = x, y = y, color = "discretized")) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = x, xend = x + 1, y = y, yend = y), color = "black") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(average_prob = "orange"),
                    labels = c(average_prob = "average probability")) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(discretized = "black"),
                     labels = c(discretized = "discretized"))
```

# Monte Carlo proposals

MCMC proposals determine how candidate parameter values are drawn at each step.
They come in two families.

*Independence samplers* draw a fresh value from a distribution:

* **forward**: direct sampling from the variable's own defining distribution;
* a **distribution name** (e.g. `"normal"`): sampling from that distribution,
  with its parameters supplied as `proposal_mean`, `proposal_sd`, ...

*Random walks* draw an increment and add it to the current value:

* **rw**: Gaussian increments: this is the default choice in housepi;
* **rw_log**: multiplicative log-normal increments (not appropriate for negative
  or discrete values);
* **rw_unif**: uniform (bounded) increments inside a window.

On a discrete variable, the increments of a random walk are rounded to the nearest integer.

## Finite adaptation

```{r}
#| label: color-scheme-proposals
#| include: false
bayesplot::color_scheme_set(scheme = "brightblue")
```

By default, housepi tunes the random walk scales to target an optimal acceptance rate [@sherlock_optimal_2009].
Only the random walks are adaptable.
The argument `adapt` of `run_inference()` sets the number of adaptation steps, run before the MCMC `steps`.
After every move, a Robbins-Monro update [@andrieu_tutorial_2008] moves the scale by the gap between
the acceptance probability of the move and the target.
This gain falls linearly to zero at the end of the adaptation, so sampling starts on a settled scale.

Without adaptation, a random walk keeps the scale it starts from, read off the prior.
That scale suits a posterior as wide as its prior, as in the "test" model above, but not one the data narrow down.
For example, if we fit the person-to-person transmission rate `beta` of the final size model to `flu_1918_frederick` under a uniform prior in $[0,\,10]$ :
```{r}
#| label: adaptation-trace
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Two trace plots of the transmission rate beta, four chains each.
#|  Without adaptation the chains stay flat for long stretches and do not overlap.
#|  With adaptation the four chains mix around the same value.
hh_model <- flu_1918_frederick |>
  new_housepi_model("final_size") |>
  add_parameter(alpha = 0.01, gamma = 1, hh_size_ref = 4,
                beta = list(prior = "uniform", max = 10, proposal = "rw"))

draws_fixed <- hh_model |> run_inference(adapt = 0) |> get_parameter_draws()
draws_adapted <- hh_model |> run_inference() |> get_parameter_draws()

posterior::bind_draws(
  posterior::rename_variables(draws_fixed, "adapt = 0" = beta),
  posterior::rename_variables(draws_adapted, "adapt = 1000" = beta),
  along = "variable"
) |>
  bayesplot::mcmc_trace(facet_args = list(ncol = 1))
```
Without adaptation, the scale is far wider than the posterior: nearly every move is rejected and the chains don't mix, as flagged by the diagnostic warning.
Adaptation shrinks the step to the width of the posterior, and the four chains mix.
